title: The Force of Truth
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Apology by Plato, translated by Benjamin Jowett (Project Gutenberg edition).
body: How you, O Athenians, have been affected by my accusers, I cannot tell; but I know that they almost made me forget who I was—so persuasively did they speak; and yet they have hardly uttered a word of truth. But of the many falsehoods told by them, there was one which quite amazed me—I mean when they said that you should be upon your guard and not allow yourselves to be deceived by the force of my eloquence. To say this, when they were certain to be detected as soon as I opened my lips and proved myself to be anything but a great speaker, did indeed appear to me most shameless—unless by the force of eloquence they mean the force of truth; for if such is their meaning, I admit that I am eloquent.

But in how different a way from theirs! Well, as I was saying, they have scarcely spoken the truth at all; but from me you shall hear the whole truth: not, however, delivered after their manner in a set oration duly ornamented with words and phrases. No, by heaven! but I shall use the words and arguments which occur to me at the moment; for I am confident in the justice of my cause: at my time of life I ought not to be appearing before you, O men of Athens, in the character of a juvenile orator—let no one expect it of me.

And first, I have to reply to the older charges and to my first accusers, and then I will go on to the later ones. For of old I have had many accusers, who have accused me falsely to you during many years; and I am more afraid of them than of Anytus and his associates, who are dangerous, too, in their own way. But far more dangerous are the others, who began when you were children, and took possession of your minds with their falsehoods, telling of one Socrates, a wise man, who speculated about the heaven above, and searched into the earth beneath, and made the worse appear the better cause.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, does Socrates say his accusers spoke the truth?
options: No, he says they hardly uttered a word of truth
Yes, he says they spoke entirely truthfully
He says only Anytus spoke truthfully
He says he cannot judge whether they spoke truthfully

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the accusers warn the jury to guard against?
options: The force of Socrates' eloquence
The wealth of Socrates' family
The influence of foreign powers
The anger of the gods

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what kind of speech does Socrates say he will NOT deliver?
options: A set oration duly ornamented with words and phrases
A short, silent gesture of apology
A speech written by Anytus
A speech delivered in a foreign language

questions.prompt: Per the passage, in what order does Socrates say he will answer his accusers?
options: He will reply to the older charges first, then the later ones
He will reply to the later charges first, then the older ones
He will answer only the charges brought by Anytus
He will refuse to answer any charges at all

questions.prompt: According to the passage, whom does Socrates say he fears more than Anytus and his associates?
options: His older, first accusers
The judges themselves
The citizens of Athens as a whole
His own former students

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did Socrates' older accusers claim he did?
options: Speculated about the heavens, searched into the earth, and made the worse argument appear the better
Stole money from the Athenian treasury
Plotted to overthrow the Athenian government
Refused to worship any gods at all

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Socrates say he admits to being eloquent, but "in how different a way from theirs"?
options: He redefines eloquence as speaking the plain truth, distinguishing it from his accusers' persuasive rhetoric
He believes eloquence is only useful for entertaining an audience
He wants to prove he is a better public speaker than Anytus
He is mocking the jury's ability to understand fine speech

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Socrates say he will use "the words and arguments which occur to me at the moment" rather than a prepared oration?
options: He wants his defense to appear unrehearsed and honest, unlike a polished, manipulative speech
He did not have enough time to prepare any kind of defense
He believes prepared speeches are illegal in Athenian courts
He hopes the jury will pity his lack of preparation

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: Socrates opens his defense by rejecting rehearsed rhetoric in favor of plain truth, and turns first to address his oldest and most dangerous accusers
Socrates begins his defense by praising the eloquence of his accusers
Socrates refuses to address any of the charges brought against him
Socrates argues that Anytus is his only accuser worth answering

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean for a speech to be a "set oration"?
options: A formal, prepared speech rehearsed in advance
A speech given while seated
A brief, informal remark
A speech translated from another language

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the accusers almost cause Socrates to do?
options: Forget who he was
Fall silent permanently
Leave the courtroom
Confess to the charges

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what does Socrates say he shall use instead of a rehearsed oration?
options: The words and arguments which occur to him at the moment
A written statement prepared by a lawyer
The exact words of his accusers
A song composed for the occasion

questions.prompt: According to the passage, in what character does Socrates say he ought not to appear, given his time of life?
options: A juvenile orator
A wise philosopher
A humble student
A foreign visitor

questions.prompt: Per the passage, whom does Socrates say he must reply to first?
options: His older charges and first accusers
Anytus and his associates alone
The jury of judges
The citizens of Athens generally

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Socrates consider his older, unnamed accusers "far more dangerous" than Anytus?
options: They shaped public opinion against him since the jurors' childhood, unopposed and unnamed, making them difficult to refute
They had more political power than Anytus in the Athenian government
They had personally threatened Socrates with violence
They were foreign agents working against Athens

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes Socrates' stated approach to his defense?
options: He will speak plainly and truthfully rather than through rehearsed rhetoric, addressing the oldest accusations first
He will refuse to speak at all until Anytus is removed from the courtroom
He will rely entirely on witnesses rather than his own words
He will focus only on the most recent charges against him

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, how does Socrates redefine "eloquence" when he admits to being eloquent?
options: As the force of truth, rather than persuasive rhetorical skill
As the ability to speak many languages
As the loudness and confidence of one's voice
As the use of complex, difficult vocabulary
